name: 1954-first-equations
tape:
# E-364 p. 2, equations (1): "Examples of such equations are"
# The PRINT and STOP are added so that the program runs.
a = 5,
y = -6.3a,
b = 0.0053 (a-y) /2ay,
PRINT a, y, b.
STOP
about:
E-364 p. 2, equations (1): "Examples of such equations are"
The PRINT and STOP are added so that the program runs.

name: 1954-division
tape:
# E-364 pp. 4-5, section 2B: how the computer reads a slash.
# "a plus or minus sign has the effect of separating any mathematical
# expression into two terms"; within a term, "a/b/c is properly interpreted
# as the product ac divided by b".
a = 1, b = 2, c = 4, d = 8,
p = a + 2b/c + d,          # (6): a, 2b/c and d: 10
q = a + 2b/(c + d),        # (7): 1.3333333
r = (a + 2b)/(c + d),      # (8): 5/12, .41666665 in 24 bits
s = cd/a(b + c) + d,       # (9): cd over a(b+c), plus d: 13.333333
u = a/b/c,                 # ac over b: 2, where FORTRAN would say .125
v = a/(b + c/d),           # (10): .4
PRINT p, q, r, s, u, v.
STOP
about:
E-364 pp. 4-5, section 2B: how the computer reads a slash.
"a plus or minus sign has the effect of separating any mathematical
expression into two terms"; within a term, "a/b/c is properly interpreted
as the product ac divided by b".

name: 1954-cosine-series
tape:
# E-364 p. 11: "print a table of values of cosine x for x = 0, .1, .2, ...,
# 1 radian ... up to the x^10 term in the power series"
x = 0,
1   z = 1 - x^2/2 + x^4/2·3·4 - x^6/2·3·4·5·6
        + x^8/2·3·4·5·6·7·8 - x^10/ 2·3·4·5·6·7·8·9·10,
    PRINT x, z.
    x = x + .1,
    e = x - 1.05,
    CP 1,
    STOP
about:
E-364 p. 11: "print a table of values of cosine x for x = 0, .1, .2, ...,
1 radian ... up to the x^10 term in the power series"

name: 1954-differential-equations
tape:
# E-364 p. 18, section 15: two differential equations,
#   dy1/dt = y2 + 1,   dy2/dt = -y1,
# from t = 2 with y1 = y2 = 0, h = 0.5, printed at t = 2, 3, ..., 10.
# Each step goes through the D equations four times (Gill's method). e = -e
# makes CP 2 take two steps for every PRINT.
    t = 2,
    h = 0.5,
    y|1 = 0,
    y|2 = 0,
1   PRINT t, y|1, y|2.
    e = 9.7 - t,
    CP 3,
2   D y|1 = y|2 + 1,
    D y|2 = - y|1,
    e = -e,
    CP 2,
    SP 1,
3   STOP
about:
E-364 p. 18, section 15: two differential equations,
  dy1/dt = y2 + 1,   dy2/dt = -y1,
from t = 2 with y1 = y2 = 0, h = 0.5, printed at t = 2, 3, ..., 10.
Each step goes through the D equations four times (Gill's method). e = -e
makes CP 2 take two steps for every PRINT.

name: 1954-innocuous-change
tape:
# E-364 p. 19: "Suppose, for example, that we were to change the part of the
# preceding program between equations 1 and 2 as follows ... This change
# would appear to be innocuous since "a" seems to be appropriately reset
# before each entry into the differential equations. However, upon
# completion of the second D equation in each of the first 3 sub-steps,
# computation would be resumed with the first D equation (and not equation
# 2) so that "a" would not have the current value of y|2 + 1."
# Compare the page with 1954-differential-equations.
    t = 2,
    h = 0.5,
    y|1 = 0,
    y|2 = 0,
1   PRINT t, y|1, y|2.
    e = 9.7 - t,
    CP 3,
2   a = y|2 + 1,
    D y|1 = a,
    D y|2 = - y|1,
    e = -e,
    CP 2,
    SP 1,
3   STOP
about:
E-364 p. 19: "Suppose, for example, that we were to change the part of the
preceding program between equations 1 and 2 as follows ... This change
would appear to be innocuous since "a" seems to be appropriately reset
before each entry into the differential equations. However, upon
completion of the second D equation in each of the first 3 sub-steps,
computation would be resumed with the first D equation (and not equation
2) so that "a" would not have the current value of y|2 + 1."
Compare the page with 1954-differential-equations.

name: 1954-zero
tape:
# E-364 p. 8: "if n has the value 3 then in the following program ... when
# the instruction CP 5, is reached the equation x = 3 ab, will be skipped ...
# If n had the value 5 in the above example then e = n - 5 = 0. In this case
# the CP may or may not behave like an SP since 0 may appear as +0 or -0."
#
# The displayed program on p. 8 has no comma after x = 3 ab (the prose
# below it writes "x = 3 ab,"), and the rules require one: it is put in here.
#
# Here n is 5. The zero is -0, CP jumps, and x is never computed: y is 0.
# lz --zero plus makes it +0: CP does not jump, x is 6 and y is 12.
a = 2, b = 1, x = 0,
n = 5,
e = n - 5,
CP 5,
x = 3 ab,
5 y = ax,
PRINT e, x, y.
STOP
about:
E-364 p. 8: "if n has the value 3 then in the following program ... when
the instruction CP 5, is reached the equation x = 3 ab, will be skipped ...
If n had the value 5 in the above example then e = n - 5 = 0. In this case
the CP may or may not behave like an SP since 0 may appear as +0 or -0."

The displayed program on p. 8 has no comma after x = 3 ab (the prose
below it writes "x = 3 ab,"), and the rules require one: it is put in here.

Here n is 5. The zero is -0, CP jumps, and x is never computed: y is 0.
lz --zero plus makes it +0: CP does not jump, x is 6 and y is 12.

name: 1976-knuth-tpk
tape:
# Knuth and Trabb Pardo, "The Early Development of Programming Languages"
# (1976), pp. 56-57: their TPK algorithm as it "would look in their system".
# Read eleven numbers, then for each in reverse order print f(t) = √|t| + 5t³,
# or 999 if that is over 400. The eleven numbers are Knuth's own example of
# the abbreviation: 1 (.5) 2 (.25) 3.5 (1) 5.5.
#
# Their ⟨input⟩ is replaced by the input they suggest on p. 57. As far as is
# known the program was never run on Whirlwind.
#
# It is incompatible with the 1954 specification in two places. Its v|N "is
# not yet in operation" (E-364 p. 21; lz --temporary-rules refuses it). And
# i comes to zero by i = i - 1 and is used as an index, which p. 13 forbids
# whatever the sign: zero is permissible only "if assigned by the specific
# equation n = 0". Here it types ten lines and then an alarm, but that alarm
# rests on this reconstruction's model of zero (a computed zero is -0), not on
# the manual, and says nothing about what Whirlwind did. lz --zero plus, a
# what-if in which every zero is +0, lets the computed zero through and runs
# it to the end.
        v|N = 1 (.5) 2 (.25) 3.5 (1) 5.5,
        i = 0,
1       j = i + 1,
        a|i = v|j,
        i = j,
        e = i - 10.5,
        CP 1,
        i = 10,
2       y = F^1(F^11(a|i)) + 5(a|i)^3,
        e = y - 400,
        CP 3,
        z = 999,
        PRINT i, z.
        SP 4,
3       PRINT i, y.
4       i = i - 1,
        e = -0.5 - i,
        CP 2,
        STOP
about:
Knuth and Trabb Pardo, "The Early Development of Programming Languages"
(1976), pp. 56-57: their TPK algorithm as it "would look in their system".
Read eleven numbers, then for each in reverse order print f(t) = √|t| + 5t³,
or 999 if that is over 400. The eleven numbers are Knuth's own example of
the abbreviation: 1 (.5) 2 (.25) 3.5 (1) 5.5.

Their ⟨input⟩ is replaced by the input they suggest on p. 57. As far as is
known the program was never run on Whirlwind.

It is incompatible with the 1954 specification in two places. Its v|N "is
not yet in operation" (E-364 p. 21; lz --temporary-rules refuses it). And
i comes to zero by i = i - 1 and is used as an index, which p. 13 forbids
whatever the sign: zero is permissible only "if assigned by the specific
equation n = 0". Here it types ten lines and then an alarm, but that alarm
rests on this reconstruction's model of zero (a computed zero is -0), not on
the manual, and says nothing about what Whirlwind did. lz --zero plus, a
what-if in which every zero is +0, lets the computed zero through and runs
it to the end.

name: 1954-alarm
tape:
# E-364 p. 20, section 16: "If an arithmetic alarm occurs, the programmer
# will be told the number of the equation in which the alarm occurred and the
# number of the equation that preceded the alarm ... The programmer may obtain
# the values of any variables he desires after an arithmetic alarm by writing
# the appropriate PRINT instruction as equation 100."
#
# The program is this repository's. Doubling x passes 2^63 - 2^39 on the
# 63rd time round. The wording of the post-mortem is made up (see README).
    x = 1,
    n = 0,
1   x = 2x,
    n = n + 1,
    SP 1,
100 PRINT n, x.
    STOP
out:
ALARM  EQUATION 1  PRECEDED BY 103

n = +.62000000+02       x = +.46116860+19
about:
E-364 p. 20, section 16: "If an arithmetic alarm occurs, the programmer
will be told the number of the equation in which the alarm occurred and the
number of the equation that preceded the alarm ... The programmer may obtain
the values of any variables he desires after an arithmetic alarm by writing
the appropriate PRINT instruction as equation 100."

The program is this repository's. Doubling x passes 2^63 - 2^39 on the
63rd time round. The wording of the post-mortem is made up (see README).

name: 1954-cosine-iterative
tape:
# E-364 p. 11: "We might prefer an iterative scheme to produce the same
# result. The following scheme has the advantage that the number of terms in
# the series may be adjusted by changing a single number"
#
# On the page, y = y - 2 ends in what looks like a semicolon (or a comma with
# a speck above it). The rules require a comma, and it is typed as one here.
    x = 0,
1   y = 10,
    z = 1,
2   z = 1 - z x^2/y (y - 1),
    y = y - 2,
    e = 1 - y,
    CP 2,
    PRINT x, z.
    x = x + 0.1,
    a = x - 1.05,
    CP 1,
    STOP
about:
E-364 p. 11: "We might prefer an iterative scheme to produce the same
result. The following scheme has the advantage that the number of terms in
the series may be adjusted by changing a single number"

On the page, y = y - 2 ends in what looks like a semicolon (or a comma with
a speck above it). The rules require a comma, and it is typed as one here.

name: 1954-counted-loop
tape:
# E-364 p. 8: "if it is desired to go thru a certain process starting with
# equation 1 exactly 10 times". e is -8.5, -7.5, ..., -0.5, +0.5: never zero.
# The manual leaves the process as dots; s = s + n, the PRINT and the STOP
# are this repository's.
    n = 0,
    s = 0,
1   s = s + n,
    n = n + 1,
    e = n - 9.5,
    CP 1,
    PRINT n, s.
    STOP
about:
E-364 p. 8: "if it is desired to go thru a certain process starting with
equation 1 exactly 10 times". e is -8.5, -7.5, ..., -0.5, +0.5: never zero.
The manual leaves the process as dots; s = s + n, the PRINT and the STOP
are this repository's.

name: 1954-drum
tape:
# E-364 pp. 15-17, section 14: variables on the drum.
ASSIGN g|4,
g|1 = 2, g|2 = 4, g|3 = 6, g|4 = 0,
# "Exactly the same thing may be accomplished by writing"
h|N = 2, 4, 6, 0,
a|N = 1.0 (.5) 2. (0.25) 2.5 (1) 4.5,
k|N = 1 (1) 10,
PRINT g|1, g|2, g|3, g|4, h|3, a|7.
PRINT k|10.
# "re-assign them to MS ... by writing something like"
    n = 0,
1   n = n + 1,
    f|n = a|n,
    e = n - 6.5,
    CP 1,
    PRINT f|1, f|2, f|3, f|4, f|5, f|6, f|7.
    STOP
about: E-364 pp. 15-17, section 14: variables on the drum.

name: 1954-exponents
tape:
# E-364 p. 5, section 2D: "Upper case numbers on the Flexowriter appear as
# exponents ... Some examples are"
#
# Chained in this order the examples go out of range. b is 1/529, ab³ is
# about 1.7·10⁻⁷, its fifth power about 10⁻³⁴ and c about 7.3·10³³: neither
# fits the 24, 6 system (2⁻⁶⁴ is about 5·10⁻²⁰, 2⁶³ about 9·10¹⁸). Here the
# power is taken first and underflows silently to zero, so (ab³)⁻⁵ is a
# division by zero; a routine that took the reciprocal first would overflow
# instead, so the particular alarm is the reconstruction's. The manual gives
# them as notation, not as a program.
a = 5²,
b = (a - 2)⁻²,
c = (ab³)⁻⁵,
d = a(b + c)²/(c - a)a⁻³,
PRINT a, b, c, d.
100 PRINT a, b.
STOP
out:
ALARM  EQUATION 103  PRECEDED BY 102

a = +.25000000+02       b = +.18903592-02
about:
E-364 p. 5, section 2D: "Upper case numbers on the Flexowriter appear as
exponents ... Some examples are"

Chained in this order the examples go out of range. b is 1/529, ab³ is
about 1.7·10⁻⁷, its fifth power about 10⁻³⁴ and c about 7.3·10³³: neither
fits the 24, 6 system (2⁻⁶⁴ is about 5·10⁻²⁰, 2⁶³ about 9·10¹⁸). Here the
power is taken first and underflows silently to zero, so (ab³)⁻⁵ is a
division by zero; a routine that took the reciprocal first would overflow
instead, so the particular alarm is the reconstruction's. The manual gives
them as notation, not as a program.

name: 1954-functions
tape:
# E-364 pp. 12-13, section 11: the function subroutines.
y = 4, z = -0.5, a = -9, b = 1,
x = 2(F^1(y) F^2(z) + F^11(z)),     # 2(√y sin z + |z|)
PRINT x.
x = F^3 (x + 2/y(a + b) z^-1),      # cos(x + 2z/y(a+b)) as the manual has it
PRINT x.
x = F^4(y + F^6(z)),                # tan(y + cos⁻¹ z)
PRINT x.
x = F^1 (F^11(a)),                  # √|a|
PRINT x.
STOP
about: E-364 pp. 12-13, section 11: the function subroutines.

name: 1954-interpolation
tape:
# E-364 pp. 13-14: linear interpolation in a table, using the rounding of a
# variable index. The table is sin x at x|1 = 0, .1, ..., .9 (the manual
# leaves the values blank).
x|1 = 0, h = .1,
f|1 = 0, f|2 = .09983342, f|3 = .19866933, f|4 = .29552021, f|5 = .38941834,
f|6 = .47942554, f|7 = .56464247, f|8 = .64421769, f|9 = .71735609, f|10 = .78332691,
# "the set of integers 1 to 10, read in as follows"
    n = 0,
1   n = n + 1,
    k|n = n,
    e = n - 9.5,
    CP 1,
# "To find f(x), (x|1 < x < x|10), by linear interpolation"
    x = .25,
    j = 0.5 + (x - x|1) /h,
    m = k|j,
    n = m + 1,
    d = j + 0.5 - m,
    y = d f|n + (1 - d) f|m,
    PRINT x, m, d, y.
    STOP
about:
E-364 pp. 13-14: linear interpolation in a table, using the rounding of a
variable index. The table is sin x at x|1 = 0, .1, ..., .9 (the manual
leaves the values blank).

name: 1954-print-layout
tape:
# E-364 pp. 6-7, section 4: six to a line, and a line space between PRINTs.
# The manual's figure for PRINT a, ..., h. shows a ninth value, i, on the
# second line: a slip in the figure. Only a to h are typed here.
a = 1, b = 2, c = 3, d = 4, e = 5, f = 6, g = 7, h = 8, i = 9,
PRINT a, b, c, d, e, f, g, h.
PRINT a,b,c. PRINT d,e,f. PRINT g,h,i.
STOP
about:
E-364 pp. 6-7, section 4: six to a line, and a line space between PRINTs.
The manual's figure for PRINT a, ..., h. shows a ninth value, i, on the
second line: a slip in the figure. Only a to h are typed here.

name: 1954-summer-session
tape:
# The 1954 MIT Summer Session notes, "Digital Computers: Advanced Coding
# Techniques", lecture 13, p. 13-3: the same two differential equations as
# E-364 p. 18, "Our program might be".
#
# As printed, k = t - 10.1 and CP 1 have no commas, which the rules require,
# so the listing as printed does not translate here; the commas are put in.
# With them it integrates from t = 2 to t = 10.5 and types nothing, because
# it has no PRINT. That need not be a mistake (a routine may leave its
# results in storage). The PRINT at the end is this repository's, added so
# that there is something to see.
    t = 2,
    h = 0.5,
    y|1 = 0,
    y|2 = 0,
1   D y|1 = y|2 + 1,
    D y|2 = -y|1,
    k = t - 10.1,
    CP 1,
    PRINT t, y|1, y|2.
    STOP
about:
The 1954 MIT Summer Session notes, "Digital Computers: Advanced Coding
Techniques", lecture 13, p. 13-3: the same two differential equations as
E-364 p. 18, "Our program might be".

As printed, k = t - 10.1 and CP 1 have no commas, which the rules require,
so the listing as printed does not translate here; the commas are put in.
With them it integrates from t = 2 to t = 10.5 and types nothing, because

name: basel
tape:
# The sum of 1/n² for n = 1 to 1000, which tends to π²/6 = 1.64493407.
# The first thousand terms come to 1.64393457 (the tail is about 1/1000).
# Added in 24 bits from n = 1 upward, the small terms near the end are partly
# lost in the large sum, and it is typed .16439348+01; added from n = 1000
# downward it is .16439346+01, one unit from the truth, .16439345+01.
    s = 0,
    n = 0,
1   n = n + 1,
    s = s + 1/n^2,
    e = n - 999.5,
    CP 1,
    PRINT s.
    s = 0,
    n = 1001,
2   n = n - 1,
    s = s + 1/n^2,
    e = 1.5 - n,
    CP 2,
    PRINT s.
    p = 3.1415927^2/6,
    PRINT p.
    STOP
about:
The sum of 1/n² for n = 1 to 1000, which tends to π²/6 = 1.64493407.
The first thousand terms come to 1.64393457 (the tail is about 1/1000).
Added in 24 bits from n = 1 upward, the small terms near the end are partly
lost in the large sum, and it is typed .16439348+01; added from n = 1000
downward it is .16439346+01, one unit from the truth, .16439345+01.

name: bisection
tape:
# The root of x³ - x - 2 = 0 between 1 and 2, by halving the interval
# twenty-four times, as far as 24 bits can go. The root is 1.52137971.
# The sign of f at the left end decides which half to keep: CP does the test.
    a = 1,
    b = 2,
    n = 0,
1   x = (a + b)/2,
    f = x^3 - x - 2,
    CP 2,
    b = x,
    SP 3,
2   a = x,
3   n = n + 1,
    e = n - 23.5,
    CP 1,
    PRINT n, a, b.
    STOP
about:
The root of x³ - x - 2 = 0 between 1 and 2, by halving the interval
twenty-four times, as far as 24 bits can go. The root is 1.52137971.
The sign of f at the left end decides which half to keep: CP does the test.

name: compound-interest
tape:
# 100 at 5 per cent a year, for ten years, and the same compounded monthly.
# After ten years: 100 · 1.05^10 = 162.88946, and 100 · (1 + .05/12)^120 =
# 164.70095. Here they are 162.88938 and 164.70204. The second is further out:
# 1 + .05/12 is rounded to 24 bits, and that error is multiplied 120 times.
    p = 100,
    r = .05,
    y = 0,
1   y = y + 1,
    p = p(1 + r),
    PRINT y, p.
    e = y - 9.5,
    CP 1,
    q = 100 (1 + r/12)^120,
    PRINT q.
    STOP
about:
100 at 5 per cent a year, for ten years, and the same compounded monthly.
After ten years: 100 · 1.05^10 = 162.88946, and 100 · (1 + .05/12)^120 =
164.70095. Here they are 162.88938 and 164.70204. The second is further out:
1 + .05/12 is rounded to 24 bits, and that error is multiplied 120 times.

name: euler-and-gill
tape:
# y' = y from y = 1 at t = 0, to t = 1, in ten steps of 0.1, two ways.
# By Euler's method, written out (y = y + hy): (1.1)^10 = 2.5937425.
# By Gill's method, which the system does for a D equation: 2.7182793, where
# e = 2.7182818. A fourth-order method with h = .1 is out by about 2·10⁻⁶ in
# exact arithmetic, so most of the difference is the method's, not the 24 bits'.
    h = 0.1,
    y = 1,
    n = 0,
1   y = y + hy,
    n = n + 1,
    e = n - 9.5,
    CP 1,
    PRINT y.
    t = 0,
    z = 1,
    n = 0,
2   Dz = z,
    n = n + 1,
    e = n - 9.5,
    CP 2,
    PRINT t, z.
    STOP
about:
y' = y from y = 1 at t = 0, to t = 1, in ten steps of 0.1, two ways.
By Euler's method, written out (y = y + hy): (1.1)^10 = 2.5937425.
By Gill's method, which the system does for a D equation: 2.7182793, where
e = 2.7182818. A fourth-order method with h = .1 is out by about 2·10⁻⁶ in
exact arithmetic, so most of the difference is the method's, not the 24 bits'.

name: exponential-table
tape:
# A table of eˣ for x = 0, .1, ..., 1 kept on the drum, and looked up by
# linear interpolation with a variable index, as on E-364 pp. 13-16.
# ASSIGN reserves g|1 to g|11 on the drum; a loop fills them with F¹³, the
# exponential; the arguments to look up are a list, u|N. e^.25 = 1.28402542 and
# e^.73 = 2.07508061; straight lines between the tabulated points come out a
# little above both.
    ASSIGN g|11,
    u|N = .25, .73,
    k|N = 1 (1) 11,
    n = 0,
1   n = n + 1,
    g|n = F^13((n - 1)/10),
    e = n - 10.5,
    CP 1,
    h = .1,
    i = 0,
2   i = i + 1,
    x = u|i,
    j = .5 + x/h,
    m = k|j,
    n = m + 1,
    d = j + .5 - m,
    y = d g|n + (1 - d) g|m,
    PRINT x, y.
    e = i - 1.5,
    CP 2,
    STOP
about:
A table of eˣ for x = 0, .1, ..., 1 kept on the drum, and looked up by
linear interpolation with a variable index, as on E-364 pp. 13-16.
ASSIGN reserves g|1 to g|11 on the drum; a loop fills them with F¹³, the
exponential; the arguments to look up are a list, u|N. e^.25 = 1.28402542 and
e^.73 = 2.07508061; straight lines between the tabulated points come out a
little above both.

name: factorial
tape:
# n! for n = 1 to 15. Up to 13! every factorial is exact in 24 bits
# (13! = 6227020800 = 6081075 · 2^10, and 6081075 is under 2^24). 14! is
# 87178291200 = 42567525 · 2^11, which needs 26 bits: from here the low digits
# are rounded away: 14! is typed .87178289+11, not .87178291+11, and
# 15! = 1307674368000 is typed .13076742+13.
    n = 0,
    f = 1,
1   n = n + 1,
    f = fn,
    PRINT n, f.
    e = n - 14.5,
    CP 1,
    STOP
about:
n! for n = 1 to 15. Up to 13! every factorial is exact in 24 bits
(13! = 6227020800 = 6081075 · 2^10, and 6081075 is under 2^24). 14! is

name: falling-body
tape:
# The simplest differential equations: a stone dropped from 100 metres.

    h = .25,

    Dv = -g,
    e = -y,

    STOP

name: gcd
tape:
# Euclid's algorithm by subtraction: the greatest common divisor of 1071 and
# 462, which is 21. The test for a = b is |a - b| - .5 < 0, with F¹¹, the
# absolute value, so that the sign of a zero difference does not matter.
    a = 1071,
    b = 462,
1   e = F^11(a - b) - .5,
    CP 4,
    e = a - b,
    CP 2,
    a = a - b,
    SP 1,
2   b = b - a,
    SP 1,
4   PRINT a, b.
    STOP

name: newton-sqrt
tape:
# Newton's method for the square root of 2: y = (y + 2/y)/2, from y = 1.
# The same iteration as E-364 p. 7 ("1 y = 0.5 (x + 2/x),"). It settles in

    a = 2,
    y = 1,
    n = 0,
1   y = 0.5 (y + a/y),

    e = n - 5.5,

    STOP

name: primes
tape:
# The primes below 50, by trial division. There is no integer part function,
# so this uses the rounding of a variable index, as E-364 p. 13 suggests: k|N
# puts the integers 1 to 60 on the drum, and k|j with j = q - .5 is the whole
# part of q. The remainder r = n - dm is tested with r - .5, never with r
# itself, because a zero remainder would be -0 (chapter 8 of the tutorial).
# Likewise d² against n + .5, so that n = 4, 9, 25, 49 are not taken for primes.
    k|N = 1 (1) 60,
    n = 2,
    PRINT n.
1   n = n + 1,
    e = n - 49.5,
    CP 2,
    SP 5,
2   d = 1,
3   d = d + 1,
    e = n + .5 - d^2,
    CP 4,
    q = n/d,
    j = q - .5,
    m = k|j,
    r = n - dm,
    e = r - .5,
    CP 1,
    SP 3,
4   PRINT n.
    SP 1,
5   STOP
about:
The primes below 50, by trial division. There is no integer part function,
so this uses the rounding of a variable index, as E-364 p. 13 suggests: k|N
puts the integers 1 to 60 on the drum, and k|j with j = q - .5 is the whole
part of q. The remainder r = n - dm is tested with r - .5, never with r
itself, because a zero remainder would be -0 (chapter 8 of the tutorial).
Likewise d² against n + .5, so that n = 4, 9, 25, 49 are not taken for primes.

name: projectile
tape:
# A shell with air resistance proportional to the square of its speed:
#   x' = u, y' = v, u' = -kus, v' = -g - kvs, with s = √(u² + v²).

# each of the four passes of a step. It flies until y goes below zero; without
# air it would land at 1019.4 after 14.4 seconds. Here it comes down between

    t = 0,
    h = 0.1,
    g = 9.81,
    k = 0.001,
    x = 0,
    y = 0,
    u = 70.710678,
    v = 70.710678,
    n = 0,
1   Dx = u,
    s = F^1(u^2 + v^2),
    Du = -kus,
    Dv = -g - kvs,
    Dy = v,
    n = n + 1,
    e = n - 9.5,
    CP 2,
    PRINT t, x, y, u, v.
    n = 0,
2   e = -y,
    CP 1,
    PRINT t, x, y.
    STOP
about:
A shell with air resistance proportional to the square of its speed:
  x' = u, y' = v, u' = -kus, v' = -g - kvs, with s = √(u² + v²).
Fired at 100 at 45 degrees, g = 9.81, k = 0.001. s is computed between the

name: pursuit
tape:
# A pursuit curve, in memory of the system's first substantial application:
# "a three-dimensional lead pursuit course flown by one aircraft attacking
# another" (Laning, 1976). This one is flat and simple. The target starts at
# (1, 0) and flies straight up the line x = 1 at speed 1. The pursuer starts at
# the origin, flies at speed w = 1.25, and always heads straight at the target:
#   x' = w(1 - x)/d,   y' = w(t - y)/d,   d = √((1 - x)² + (t - y)²).
# The square root is written into each D equation, because the first D
# equation needs it and auxiliary computation must come after the first D
# equation (E-364 p. 19). Theory says the pursuer catches the target at
# t = w/(w² - 1) = 2.2222222, at height 2.2222222. The program stops when the
# distance d is under .03, at t = 2.12; by then the pursuer is right behind
# the target and closes at w - 1 = .25 a second, so the last .0256 takes
# another .10: caught at about 2.22, as theory says.
    t = 0,
    h = 0.02,
    w = 1.25,
    x = 0,
    y = 0,
    n = 0,
1   Dx = w(1 - x)/F^1((1 - x)^2 + (t - y)^2),
    Dy = w(t - y)/F^1((1 - x)^2 + (t - y)^2),
    d = F^1((1 - x)^2 + (t - y)^2),
    n = n + 1,
    e = n - 9.5,
    CP 2,
    n = 0,
    PRINT t, x, y, d.
2   e = d - .03,
    CP 3,
    SP 1,
3   PRINT t, x, y, d.
    STOP
about:
A pursuit curve, in memory of the system's first substantial application:
"a three-dimensional lead pursuit course flown by one aircraft attacking
another" (Laning, 1976). This one is flat and simple. The target starts at
(1, 0) and flies straight up the line x = 1 at speed 1. The pursuer starts at
the origin, flies at speed w = 1.25, and always heads straight at the target:
  x' = w(1 - x)/d,   y' = w(t - y)/d,   d = √((1 - x)² + (t - y)²).
The square root is written into each D equation, because the first D
equation needs it and auxiliary computation must come after the first D
equation (E-364 p. 19). Theory says the pursuer catches the target at
t = w/(w² - 1) = 2.2222222, at height 2.2222222. The program stops when the
distance d is under .03, at t = 2.12; by then the pursuer is right behind
the target and closes at w - 1 = .25 a second, so the last .0256 takes
another .10: caught at about 2.22, as theory says.

name: simpson
tape:
# Simpson's rule for the integral of 4/(1 + x²) from 0 to 1, which is π, with
# ten strips. The weights go 1, 4, 2, 4, ..., 2, 4, 1; w = 6 - w turns 4 into 2
# and back. π = 3.14159265; Simpson with ten strips gives 3.14159261 in exact
# arithmetic.
    m = 10,
    h = 1/m,
    s = 4 + 2,          # the ends: 4/(1 + 0) and 4/(1 + 1)
    w = 4,
    i = 0,
1   i = i + 1,
    x = ih,
    s = s + 4w/(1 + x^2),
    w = 6 - w,
    e = i - m + 1.5,
    CP 1,
    p = sh/3,
    PRINT p.
    STOP
about:
Simpson's rule for the integral of 4/(1 + x²) from 0 to 1, which is π, with
ten strips. The weights go 1, 4, 2, 4, ..., 2, 4, 1; w = 6 - w turns 4 into 2
and back. π = 3.14159265; Simpson with ten strips gives 3.14159261 in exact

1   x = dr,

name: sr-and-cr
tape:
# SR and CR (E-364 p. 9): "SR 5, causes equation 5 to be executed next and
# then, after equation 5, the equation or instruction following the SR 5". It
# carries out one equation, not a group of them. CR does the same only when
# the last computed quantity is negative.
#
# Here equation 50 squares x, and is borrowed by SR three times; equation 60
# makes y positive, and is borrowed by CR only when y is negative.
    x = 2,
    SR 50,
    SR 50,
    SR 50,
    PRINT x.
    y = -7,
    CR 60,
    PRINT y.
    y = 3,
    CR 60,
    PRINT y.
    SP 70,
50  x = x^2,
60  y = -y,
70  STOP
about:

then, after equation 5, the equation or instruction following the SR 5". It
carries out one equation, not a group of them. CR does the same only when
the last computed quantity is negative.

Here equation 50 squares x, and is borrowed by SR three times; equation 60
makes y positive, and is borrowed by CR only when y is negative.
